--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Parity

For any integer \(x\)

\[
x^{3}+3x= x\,(x^{2}+3)\equiv0\pmod 2 ,
\]

hence \(x^{3}+3x+2\) is always even and \(n\ge 1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  \(x\) cannot be odd  

If \(x\) is odd, write \(x=2k+1\;(k\ge 0)\).  Then  

\[
x^{3}+3x+2\equiv 1+3+2\equiv 2\pmod 4.
\]

But a power of two is congruent to \(2\pmod 4\) only for \(2^{1}=2\).
Thus an odd \(x\) would force \(2^{n}=2\), i.e.  

\[
x^{3}+3x+2=2\Longrightarrow x(x^{2}+3)=0,
\]

which gives the (non‑odd) solution \(x=0\).  Hence **every solution with
\(x>0\) must have \(x\) even**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Reduce to an equation for a half‑integer

Put \(x=2k\;(k\ge 0)\).  Then

\[
(2k)^{3}+3(2k)+2=8k^{3}+6k+2=2\bigl(4k^{3}+3k+1\bigr)=2^{n}.
\]

Consequently  

\[
4k^{3}+3k+1=2^{\,n-1}\qquad (n\ge 1). \tag{1}
\]

Denote the left–hand side of (1) by \(f(k)=4k^{3}+3k+1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  \(k\) cannot be even (except \(k=0\))

If \(k\) is even, write \(k=2t\).  Then

\[
f(k)=4(8t^{3})+3(2t)+1=32t^{3}+6t+1\equiv 6t+1\pmod 8,
\]

so \(f(k)\equiv1\) or \(7\pmod 8\).  For a power of two to be \(\ge8\) it
must be \(0\pmod 8\); thus (1) has no solution with even \(k>0\).
The only even possibility is \(k=0\), which gives \(x=0,\;n=1\).

Hence **for any solution with \(x>0\) we must have \(k\) odd**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  First descent step (odd \(k\))

Write \(k=2t+1\;(t\ge0)\).
Substituting into \(f(k)\) gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
f(k) &=4(2t+1)^{3}+3(2t+1)+1\\
     &=2\bigl(16t^{3}+24t^{2}+15t+4\bigr)  \\
     &=2\,g(t),
\end{aligned}
\]

where \(g(t)=16t^{3}+24t^{2}+15t+4\).

Equation (1) becomes  

\[
2\,g(t)=2^{\,n-1}\Longrightarrow g(t)=2^{\,n-2}. \tag{2}
\]

If \(t\) were odd, then \(g(t)\) would be odd (since the three terms
containing \(t\) are odd and the constant term \(4\) is even), and
\(g(t)>1\).  An odd integer \(>1\) cannot be a power of two, so **\(t\)
must be even**.  Write \(t=2s\); then \(k=4s+1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Second descent step

With \(t=2s\),

\[
g(t)=16(8s^{3})+24(4s^{2})+15(2s)+4
     =2\bigl(64s^{3}+48s^{2}+15s+2\bigr)
     =2\,h(s),
\]

where \(h(s)=64s^{3}+48s^{2}+15s+2\).

Equation (2) now reads  

\[
2\,h(s)=2^{\,n-2}\Longrightarrow h(s)=2^{\,n-3}. \tag{3}
\]

Again, if \(s\) were odd, \(h(s)\) would be odd \((>1)\), impossible.
Hence **\(s\) must be even**; write \(s=2u\).  Then \(k=8u+1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  Infinite descent

Repeating the same argument we obtain the chain

\[
k=2t+1,\;t=2s,\;s=2u,\;u=2v,\dots
\]

Thus a solution with \(k>0\) forces  

\[
k\equiv1\pmod{2},\;k\equiv1\pmod{4},\;k\equiv1\pmod{8},\;
k\equiv1\pmod{16},\dots
\]

i.e. \(k\equiv1\pmod{2^{r}}\) for every \(r\).  The only integer that
satisfies all these congruences is \(k=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8.  Determining \(x\) and \(n\)

Thus the only positive solution of (1) is \(k=1\).  Consequently  

\[
x=2k=2,\qquad 
4k^{3}+3k+1=4+3+1=8=2^{3},
\]

so \(n-1=3\) and \(n=4\).  Indeed

\[
2^{3}+3\cdot2+2=8+6+2=16=2^{4}.
\]

Together with the trivial solution obtained from \(k=0\) (\(x=0,\;n=1\))
we have found **all** natural‑number solutions.
